notes:
# Animal vs plant cells

| Structure | Function | Animal | Plant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cell membrane | Controls what enters and leaves | ✓ | ✓ |
| Cytoplasm | Jelly where chemical reactions happen | ✓ | ✓ |
| Nucleus | Contains DNA/chromosomes; controls the cell | ✓ | ✓ |
| Mitochondria | Aerobic respiration → releases energy | ✓ | ✓ |
| Ribosomes | Make proteins | ✓ | ✓ |
| Cell wall | Cellulose; support and shape | ✗ | ✓ |
| Chloroplasts | Contain chlorophyll; photosynthesis | ✗ | ✓ |
| Large permanent vacuole | Cell sap; keeps cell turgid | ✗ | ✓ |

> Bacterial cells: cell wall (not cellulose), cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, **circular DNA + plasmids**, no nucleus.

# Levels of organisation

**Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism**

- **Tissue:** a group of similar cells doing the same job (muscle tissue, xylem).
- **Organ:** several tissues working together (heart, leaf).
- **Organ system:** organs working together (digestive system).

# Specialised cells

| Cell | Adaptation | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Ciliated cell | Hair-like cilia that beat | Move mucus up the airways |
| Root hair cell | Long extension → large surface area | Absorb water and mineral ions |
| Xylem vessel | Hollow tube, no cytoplasm, lignin walls | Transport water; support |
| Palisade mesophyll | Many chloroplasts, packed at top of leaf | Photosynthesis |
| Nerve cell (neurone) | Very long, insulated | Carry electrical impulses |
| Red blood cell | No nucleus, biconcave, haemoglobin | Carry oxygen |
| Sperm cell | Tail, many mitochondria, enzymes in head | Swim to and fertilise the egg |
| Egg cell | Large, energy store, jelly coat | Nutrition for the embryo |

# Magnification

**Magnification = image size ÷ actual size**

- Rearrange: actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
- Both measurements must be in the **same units** before dividing (1 mm = 1000 µm).
- Magnification has no units; write it as ×400.

Example: a cell image is 40 mm wide; actual cell is 0.05 mm → magnification = 40 ÷ 0.05 = ×800.

notes:
# 1.1 Characteristics of living organisms — MRS GREN

| | Process | Definition (learn word for word) |
|---|---|---|
| **M** | Movement | An action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place |
| **R** | Respiration | The chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism |
| **S** | Sensitivity | The ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment |
| **G** | Growth | A permanent increase in size and dry mass |
| **R** | Reproduction | The processes that make more of the same kind of organism |
| **E** | Excretion | The removal of the waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements |
| **N** | Nutrition | The taking in of materials for energy, growth and development |

> A car moves, uses fuel and gives off waste, but it does not grow, reproduce or respond — it is not alive. All seven are needed.

# 1.2 Concept and use of a classification system

## Carl Linnaeus — the father of classification

- **Carl Linnaeus** (1707–1778), a Swedish botanist and doctor, published *Systema Naturae* in **1735**.
- He invented the **binomial system** of naming (two Latin names: genus + species) that we still use, replacing long descriptive names that differed from country to country.
- He grouped organisms into a **hierarchy** of ranks (kingdom → class → order → genus → species; phylum and family were added later) based on **shared physical features** (morphology).
- His system was **artificial** — based on appearance only. Modern classification is **natural**, based on evolutionary relationships shown by DNA. Linnaeus grouped whales with fish at first; DNA shows they are mammals.

> Why it matters: before Linnaeus, the same plant could have five different names in five countries. One agreed Latin name lets scientists everywhere know exactly which organism is meant.

- Organisms are classified into groups by the **features they share**.
- **Species:** a group of organisms that can reproduce to produce **fertile** offspring. (A horse and a donkey produce a mule, which is infertile — so they are different species.)
- **Binomial system:** an internationally agreed system in which the scientific name of an organism is made up of two parts: the **genus** and the **species**.
  - Genus first with a capital letter, species second in lowercase; the whole name in *italics* (or underlined when handwritten): *Homo sapiens*, *Panthera leo*.
  - Why? The same name is used worldwide in every language; it shows which organisms are closely related (same genus).
- **Hierarchy of classification** (biggest to smallest): Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. *"King Philip Came Over For Good Soup."*
- **Dichotomous keys:** a series of paired statements; at each step you choose the one that matches, until you reach the name. Used to identify unfamiliar organisms.

## Classification and evolution

- Traditionally, classification used **morphology** (shape) and **anatomy** (internal structure).
- Now scientists use **DNA base sequences** and the **amino acid sequences of proteins**. Organisms that share a more recent common ancestor have more similar DNA sequences → this reveals **evolutionary relationships** more accurately than appearance.

# 1.3 Features of organisms

## Features of all living organisms

All living things are made of **cells**. Cells contain cytoplasm, a cell membrane, ribosomes, enzymes and DNA as genetic material.

## The five kingdoms

| Kingdom | Cell type | Cell wall | Nutrition | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Animals** | Multicellular, nucleus | None | Heterotrophic (eat other organisms); most have nervous coordination and can move | Humans, insects, fish |
| **Plants** | Multicellular, nucleus | Cellulose | Autotrophic (photosynthesis); chloroplasts; store starch | Moss, ferns, flowering plants |
| **Fungi** | Multicellular (or unicellular yeast), nucleus, made of hyphae | Chitin (not cellulose) | Saprotrophic (secrete enzymes onto dead matter, absorb the products) or parasitic | Mushrooms, mould, yeast |
| **Protoctists** | Mostly unicellular, nucleus | Some have | Some photosynthesise (algae), some feed like animals | Amoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium (malaria) |
| **Prokaryotes** | Unicellular, **no nucleus**; circular DNA + plasmids | Yes (not cellulose) | Various | Bacteria, e.g. E. coli |

**Viruses** are not in any kingdom: not made of cells, only a protein coat around genetic material (DNA or RNA), and can only reproduce inside a host cell → not considered living.

## Animal kingdom

### Vertebrates (backbone)

| Class | Body covering | Breathing | Reproduction | Temperature | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fish | Scales | Gills | Eggs in water (external fertilisation) | Cold-blooded | Salmon |
| Amphibians | Moist smooth skin | Gills as larvae, lungs + skin as adults | Eggs in water | Cold-blooded | Frog |
| Reptiles | Dry scaly skin | Lungs | Soft-shelled eggs on land | Cold-blooded | Snake, lizard |
| Birds | Feathers, beak, wings | Lungs | Hard-shelled eggs | Warm-blooded | Eagle |
| Mammals | Hair/fur | Lungs | Live young; feed milk from mammary glands | Warm-blooded | Human, whale |

### Arthropods (invertebrates with jointed legs and an exoskeleton)

| Group | Legs | Body parts | Antennae | Other | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Insects | 6 (3 pairs) | 3 (head, thorax, abdomen) | 1 pair | Usually 2 pairs of wings | Butterfly, ant |
| Arachnids | 8 (4 pairs) | 2 (cephalothorax, abdomen) | None | Many have simple eyes | Spider, scorpion |
| Crustaceans | 10 or more (5+ pairs) | 2 | 2 pairs | Hard shell, mostly aquatic | Crab, woodlouse |
| Myriapods | Many (1 or 2 pairs per segment) | Many segments | 1 pair | Long bodies | Centipede, millipede |

## Plant kingdom

- **Ferns:** roots, stems and leaves (fronds); no flowers; reproduce with **spores** on the underside of leaves.
- **Flowering plants:** roots, stems, leaves, flowers; reproduce with **seeds** inside fruits.

| | Monocotyledons | Dicotyledons |

| Seed leaves (cotyledons) | One | Two |
| Leaf veins | Parallel | Branching network |
| Flower parts | In multiples of 3 | In multiples of 4 or 5 |
| Roots | Fibrous | Tap root |
| Examples | Grass, wheat, maize, lily | Bean, rose, oak, sunflower |

# 1.4 Dichotomous keys

"Dichotomous" means **dividing into two**. Each step gives two contrasting statements; you pick the one that fits and follow it.

## Using a key

1. Start at statement 1; decide which of the two options matches your organism.
2. Follow the instruction at the end of that line (go to another number, or read the name).
3. Repeat until you reach a name. Always start again from 1 for the next organism.

Example key for four arthropods:

```
1 a  Has wings ........................ go to 2
  b  No wings ......................... go to 3
2 a  One pair of wings ................ housefly
  b  Two pairs of wings ............... butterfly
3 a  Six legs ......................... ant
  b  Eight legs ....................... spider
```

## Constructing (making) a key — step by step

1. **List** the organisms and draw up a table of their **observable features** (legs, wings, antennae, shell, body segments, leaf shape, flower colour count…).
2. Pick a feature that **splits the group into two** (ideally roughly in half). Write it as a pair of **contrasting** statements: *a) has a shell / b) no shell*.
3. For each half, pick another feature that splits it again. Keep going until every branch ends with **one organism**.
4. Number the steps and add "go to …" instructions or the organism's name.
5. **Check** by running every organism through the key — each must reach the correct name and only that name.

**Rules for good statements**

- Use features that are **fixed and easy to observe**: number of legs, wings present/absent, leaf edge smooth/toothed, shape.
- **Avoid** size, colour, behaviour, habitat or anything that changes with age or environment ("big", "green", "lives in water").
- Both statements in a pair must be about the **same feature** and must be **opposites** ("has fins / no fins", not "has fins / has legs").
- Use **yes/no** or **either/or** wording, never "usually" or "sometimes".
- A key for *n* organisms needs **n − 1** pairs of statements.

**Worked example** — make a key for: oak leaf (lobed edge, single leaf), holly leaf (spiky edge, single, shiny), rose leaf (toothed edge, made of several leaflets), pine (needle-shaped).

```
1 a  Leaf needle-shaped ............... pine
  b  Leaf flat and broad .............. go to 2
2 a  Leaf made of several leaflets .... rose
  b  Leaf is a single blade ........... go to 3
3 a  Edge has spikes .................. holly
  b  Edge is lobed (rounded) .......... oak
```

Four organisms → three pairs of statements ✓. Every organism is reached ✓. No colour or size used ✓.

**Keys can also be drawn as a branching diagram** (a "tree"): each branch point is one pair of statements. The exam may ask you to convert between the two forms.

> **Exam tip:** in a question comparing groups, quote **two or three specific features** from the tables above, e.g. "insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts; arachnids have 8 legs and 2 body parts".

notes:
# 5.1 What enzymes are

- A **catalyst** is a substance that **speeds up a chemical reaction without being changed or used up**.
- **Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts.** They speed up the reactions of metabolism (respiration, photosynthesis, digestion, building proteins) at body temperature; without them these reactions would be far too slow for life.
- The molecule an enzyme acts on is the **substrate**; what is made is the **product**.

| Enzyme | Substrate | Product |
|---|---|---|
| Amylase | Starch | Maltose (a sugar) |
| Protease | Protein | Amino acids |
| Lipase | Fats | Fatty acids + glycerol |
| Catalase | Hydrogen peroxide | Water + oxygen |

# 5.2 How enzymes work — the lock and key model

- Each enzyme has an **active site** with a specific 3-D shape.
- Only a substrate with the **complementary** shape fits, like a key in a lock → enzymes are **specific** (amylase only breaks down starch).
- Substrate binds → **enzyme–substrate complex** → reaction happens → products leave → the enzyme is unchanged and can be used again.

# 5.3 Effect of temperature

- **Low temperature:** molecules move slowly, few collisions between enzyme and substrate → slow reaction.
- **Rising temperature:** more kinetic energy, more frequent and more energetic collisions → rate increases (roughly doubles every 10 °C).
- **Optimum temperature:** fastest rate — about **37 °C** for human enzymes.
- **Above the optimum:** the enzyme's shape (especially the active site) is changed by the heat → substrate no longer fits → the enzyme is **denatured**. Denaturing is **permanent**. Rate falls quickly to zero.

> Cold does **not** denature enzymes — it just slows them. Warming them up again restores activity. Heat denaturation cannot be reversed.

# 5.4 Effect of pH

- Each enzyme has an **optimum pH**. Most work best around pH 7; **pepsin** (stomach protease) works best at **pH 2**; enzymes in the small intestine prefer pH 8.
- Moving away from the optimum changes the charges on the enzyme, altering the active site → activity falls; extreme pH **denatures** it.

Both graphs (rate vs temperature, rate vs pH) are **bell-shaped** with a peak at the optimum; the temperature curve is asymmetric (steep drop above the optimum).

# 5.5 Investigating enzymes

**Amylase and starch:** mix amylase with starch solution in water baths at different temperatures; every 30 s take a drop and add to iodine on a spotting tile; the time until iodine **stays orange-brown** (no starch left) is the reaction time. Shorter time = faster enzyme. Rate = 1 ÷ time.

**Catalase and hydrogen peroxide:** potato or liver pieces in hydrogen peroxide; measure the **volume of oxygen** collected in a set time, or the height of foam. Repeat at different temperatures/pH.

**Fair test variables:** keep concentrations, volumes and time the same; change only one factor; use a **control** (boiled enzyme) to show the enzyme is causing the change.

notes:
# 7.1 Diet

A **balanced diet** contains the right amounts of all nutrients for age, sex and activity level.

| Nutrient | Main sources | Why needed | Deficiency |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Carbohydrates** | Bread, rice, potatoes, sugar | Energy (respiration) | Lack of energy |
| **Fats** | Butter, oils, nuts | Energy store, insulation, cell membranes | — |
| **Proteins** | Meat, fish, eggs, beans | Growth and repair, enzymes, antibodies | **Kwashiorkor** (swollen belly, stunted growth) |
| **Vitamin C** | Citrus fruit, peppers | Healthy skin, gums, wound healing | **Scurvy** (bleeding gums) |
| **Vitamin D** | Oily fish, eggs, sunlight on skin | Absorbing calcium → strong bones | **Rickets** (soft, bent bones) |
| **Calcium** | Milk, cheese, green vegetables | Bones and teeth, blood clotting | Rickets, weak bones |
| **Iron** | Red meat, liver, spinach | Making **haemoglobin** | **Anaemia** (tiredness, pale) |
| **Fibre (roughage)** | Vegetables, wholegrain cereals | Adds bulk, prevents **constipation** | Constipation, bowel problems |
| **Water** | Drinks, food | Solvent, transport, sweating | Dehydration |

**Malnutrition** = an unbalanced diet: starvation, **obesity** (too much energy intake → heart disease, diabetes), **coronary heart disease** (too much saturated fat/cholesterol blocks coronary arteries).

# 7.2 The alimentary canal (digestive system)

**Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine (duodenum, ileum) → large intestine (colon, rectum) → anus.** Associated organs: salivary glands, liver, gall bladder, pancreas.

| Part | What happens |
|---|---|
| Mouth | Teeth chew (**mechanical digestion**); saliva contains **amylase** (starch → maltose); food formed into a bolus |
| Oesophagus | **Peristalsis** — waves of muscle contraction push food along |
| Stomach | Muscular churning; **hydrochloric acid** kills bacteria and gives pH 2 for **pepsin** (protease: protein → polypeptides) |
| Duodenum | **Bile** from the liver (stored in the gall bladder) neutralises acid and **emulsifies fats** (breaks into droplets → larger surface area for lipase); **pancreatic juice**: amylase, trypsin (protease), lipase |
| Ileum | Enzymes in the wall finish digestion (maltase: maltose → glucose); **absorption** of nutrients |
| Colon | Absorbs **water** |
| Rectum / anus | Faeces stored, then egested |

**Key definitions**

- **Ingestion:** taking food into the body. **Digestion:** breaking large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones. **Absorption:** movement of digested food molecules through the wall of the intestine into the blood. **Assimilation:** using absorbed molecules in cells. **Egestion:** removing undigested food as faeces.
- **Mechanical digestion:** breaking food into smaller pieces without chemical change (teeth, stomach churning) — increases surface area. **Chemical digestion:** enzymes break large molecules into small ones.

# 7.3 Enzymes of digestion

| Enzyme | Where made | Substrate → Product |
|---|---|---|
| Amylase | Salivary glands, pancreas | Starch → maltose |
| Maltase | Small intestine wall | Maltose → glucose |
| Protease (pepsin, trypsin) | Stomach, pancreas | Protein → amino acids |
| Lipase | Pancreas | Fats → fatty acids + glycerol |

# 7.4 Absorption — the small intestine is adapted

- Very **long** (about 5 m) and lined with millions of **villi** (finger-like projections) with **microvilli** → **huge surface area**.
- Wall one cell thick → **short diffusion distance**.
- Rich blood supply (**capillaries**) maintains the concentration gradient; **lacteal** in each villus absorbs fats into the lymph.
- Absorption by diffusion **and active transport**.

# 7.5 Teeth

- **Incisors** (cut), **canines** (tear), **premolars and molars** (grind). Structure: enamel (hardest substance in the body), dentine, pulp (nerves, blood), cement, root.
- **Tooth decay:** bacteria in plaque feed on sugar → **acid** dissolves enamel → cavity reaches dentine and pulp (pain). Prevention: brush with **fluoride** toothpaste, less sugar, regular dentist visits.

notes:
# Definitions the mark scheme wants

These are the exact definitions from the Cambridge IGCSE Biology (0610) syllabus for the first three units. If a question says **"Define"** or **"State what is meant by"**, write these.

## Unit 1 — Characteristics & classification

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Movement** | An action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place |
| **Respiration** | The chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism |
| **Sensitivity** | The ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment |
| **Growth** | A permanent increase in size and dry mass |
| **Reproduction** | The processes that make more of the same kind of organism |
| **Excretion** | The removal of the waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements |
| **Nutrition** | The taking in of materials for energy, growth and development |
| **Species** | A group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring |
| **Binomial system** | An internationally agreed system in which the scientific name of an organism is made up of two parts showing the genus and species |
| **Dichotomous key** | A way of identifying organisms using a series of paired, contrasting statements |
| **Vertebrate** | An animal with a backbone |
| **Arthropod** | An invertebrate with jointed legs and an exoskeleton |

## Unit 2 — Cells

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Cell membrane** | Partially permeable layer that controls what enters and leaves the cell |
| **Cell wall** | Rigid layer of cellulose around plant cells that gives support and shape |
| **Cytoplasm** | Jelly-like substance where chemical reactions take place |
| **Nucleus** | Contains the genetic material (chromosomes/DNA) and controls cell activities |
| **Mitochondrion** | Organelle where aerobic respiration takes place, releasing energy |
| **Ribosome** | Site of protein synthesis |
| **Chloroplast** | Organelle containing chlorophyll where photosynthesis takes place |
| **Vacuole** | Space filled with cell sap; keeps the plant cell turgid |
| **Tissue** | A group of cells with similar structures, working together to perform a shared function |
| **Organ** | A structure made up of a group of tissues, working together to perform specific functions |
| **Organ system** | A group of organs with related functions, working together to perform body functions |
| **Magnification** | Image size ÷ actual size |

## Unit 3 — Movement into and out of cells

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Diffusion** | The net movement of particles from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, as a result of their random movement |
| **Osmosis** | The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential (dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (concentrated solution), through a partially permeable membrane |
| **Active transport** | The movement of particles through a cell membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration (against a concentration gradient), using energy from respiration |
| **Partially permeable membrane** | A membrane that lets some molecules (e.g. water) through but not others |
| **Turgid** | A plant cell that is firm because it is full of water; the contents push against the cell wall |
| **Flaccid** | A plant cell that has lost water and is soft |
| **Plasmolysis** | The cell membrane and cytoplasm pull away from the cell wall as a plant cell loses water |
| **Concentration gradient** | The difference in concentration between two regions |

> **Trick for the three transport processes:** diffusion = *anything*, high → low, no energy; osmosis = *water only*, through a membrane, no energy; active transport = low → high, *needs energy*.

notes:
# 4.1 The chemicals of life

| Molecule | Elements | Built from | Examples & uses |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Carbohydrates** | C, H, O | Simple sugars (glucose) | Glucose (energy in respiration), sucrose, starch (plant energy store), glycogen (animal store), cellulose (plant cell walls) |
| **Proteins** | C, H, O, N (sometimes S) | Amino acids (about 20 kinds) joined in chains | Enzymes, haemoglobin, antibodies, muscle, keratin; the **sequence** of amino acids gives each protein its 3-D shape |
| **Lipids (fats and oils)** | C, H, O | 1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids | Energy store, insulation, cell membranes, waterproofing |

**Large molecules from small ones:**

- glucose × many → **starch, glycogen, cellulose**
- amino acids × many → **protein**
- fatty acids + glycerol → **fat / oil**

# 4.2 Water

About 70% of a cell is water. It is a **solvent**: chemical reactions happen in solution, substances are transported dissolved in it (blood plasma, xylem sap), and it is needed for digestion, excretion (urine) and cooling (sweat).

# 4.3 DNA

- **DNA** (deoxyribonucleic acid) carries the genetic code.
- Two strands coiled into a **double helix**.
- Each strand is a chain of **nucleotides**; each nucleotide has a **base**: A, T, C, G.
- The bases pair across the strands: **A with T, C with G** (complementary base pairing).
- The **sequence of bases** codes for the sequence of amino acids in a protein.

# 4.4 Food tests — learn the reagent, colour change and method

| Test for | Reagent | Method | Positive result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Starch** | Iodine solution | Add a few drops to the food | Orange-brown → **blue-black** |
| **Reducing sugars** (e.g. glucose) | **Benedict's** solution | Add to food solution, **heat in a water bath** (80 °C) | Blue → green → yellow → orange → **brick red** (more red = more sugar) |
| **Protein** | **Biuret** solution (copper sulfate + sodium hydroxide) | Add to food solution, shake, no heating | Blue → **purple / lilac** |
| **Fats / lipids** | **Ethanol** then water (emulsion test) | Shake food with ethanol, pour into water | Clear → **cloudy white emulsion** |
| **Vitamin C** | **DCPIP** solution (blue) | Add food juice drop by drop | Blue → **colourless** (fewer drops = more vitamin C) |

> **Exam wording:** always give the colour **before and after**. "Benedict's turns brick red" is not enough — "Benedict's changes from blue to brick red when heated" gets the marks.

**Safety:** Benedict's test needs a water bath, not a direct flame; ethanol is flammable; biuret contains sodium hydroxide (corrosive) — wear goggles.

notes:
# 6.1 Photosynthesis

**Definition:** the process by which plants synthesise carbohydrates from raw materials (carbon dioxide and water) using energy from light.

**Word equation:** carbon dioxide + water → (light, chlorophyll) → glucose + oxygen

**Balanced symbol equation:** **6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂**

- **Chlorophyll** (green pigment in chloroplasts) **absorbs light energy** and transfers it into chemical energy in glucose.
- Photosynthesis happens mainly in the **palisade mesophyll** cells of leaves.

## What the plant does with glucose

- Used in **respiration** for energy.
- Stored as **starch** (insoluble, so it doesn't affect osmosis) in leaves, roots, tubers.
- Made into **cellulose** for cell walls, **sucrose** for transport in the phloem.
- Combined with **nitrate ions** to make **amino acids → proteins**.

# 6.2 Leaf structure — adapted for photosynthesis

| Part | Adaptation |
|---|---|
| Large, flat, thin shape | Large surface area to absorb light; short diffusion distance for CO₂ |
| Waxy cuticle | Waterproof, reduces water loss |
| Upper epidermis | Transparent — lets light through |
| Palisade mesophyll | Column-shaped cells packed with chloroplasts, near the top for maximum light |
| Spongy mesophyll | Air spaces let CO₂ diffuse to cells |
| Stomata (mostly on the lower surface) | Pores that let CO₂ in and O₂ out; opened/closed by guard cells |
| Vascular bundle (veins) | Xylem brings water; phloem carries away sugars |

# 6.3 Experiments

**Testing a leaf for starch** (shows photosynthesis has happened): 1 boil the leaf in water (kills it, softens it); 2 boil in **ethanol** in a water bath (removes chlorophyll — flame off, ethanol is flammable); 3 rinse in warm water (softens); 4 spread out, add **iodine** → blue-black where starch is present.

- **Destarch** the plant first: 48 hours in the dark so old starch is used up.
- **Light needed:** cover part of a leaf with foil → only the uncovered part goes blue-black.
- **Chlorophyll needed:** variegated leaf (green and white) → only the green parts go blue-black.
- **CO₂ needed:** plant in a sealed bag with **soda lime** (absorbs CO₂) → no starch.
- **Oxygen produced:** pondweed under a funnel and test tube; bubbles collect; a **glowing splint relights**.

# 6.4 Limiting factors

The rate of photosynthesis is limited by whichever factor is in **shortest supply**: **light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature**.

- Raise light intensity → rate rises → then **levels off** (graph goes flat) because something else (CO₂ or temperature) is now limiting.
- Greenhouses add CO₂, heaters and lamps to raise all three.
- Measuring rate: count bubbles from pondweed per minute (or volume of gas) at different lamp distances; light intensity ∝ 1/distance².

# 6.5 Mineral ions

| Ion | Needed for | Deficiency symptom |
|---|---|---|
| **Nitrate (NO₃⁻)** | Making amino acids → proteins (growth) | Stunted growth, yellow older leaves |
| **Magnesium (Mg²⁺)** | Making **chlorophyll** | Yellow leaves (chlorosis) |

Absorbed from soil by root hairs, mostly by **active transport**.

notes:
# 8.1 Xylem and phloem

| | Xylem | Phloem |
|---|---|---|
| Transports | **Water and mineral ions** | **Sucrose and amino acids** |
| Direction | **Up only** — roots → stem → leaves | **Both ways** — from leaves (source) to wherever needed (sink: roots, fruits, growing tips) |
| Structure | Dead, hollow tubes with no end walls; thick walls strengthened with **lignin** | Living cells (sieve tubes) with sieve plates; companion cells |
| Also | Gives **support** | — |

- **Translocation** = movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem.
- Together xylem and phloem form **vascular bundles**: in the **root** the xylem is a central X/star with phloem between the arms; in the **stem** bundles are arranged in a ring near the outside (support); in the **leaf** they are the veins (xylem on top, phloem below).

# 8.2 Water uptake

1. Water enters **root hair cells** by **osmosis** (soil water has a higher water potential than the cell).
2. Root hairs: long thin extensions → **large surface area**; thin walls; many of them.
3. Water moves across the root cortex cell to cell (osmosis) into the **xylem**.
4. **Mineral ions** are absorbed by **active transport** (against the gradient, using energy) — root hair cells have many mitochondria.

**Experiment:** put a plant (or celery) in water with a coloured dye; after some hours cut the stem — the dye is only in the xylem, showing the pathway.

# 8.3 Transpiration

**Definition:** the **loss of water vapour** from the leaves through the **stomata** by evaporation from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells followed by diffusion out of the leaf.

**How water moves up the plant (the transpiration stream):**

- Water evaporates from the spongy mesophyll cells into the air spaces and diffuses out through the stomata.
- This pulls water out of the xylem in the leaf; water molecules stick together (**cohesion**), so a continuous column is pulled up the xylem from the roots — the **transpiration pull**.

**Factors that increase the rate of transpiration**

| Factor | Effect | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Higher **temperature** | Faster | More evaporation, faster diffusion |
| Lower **humidity** | Faster | Steeper water-vapour concentration gradient out of the leaf |
| **Wind** | Faster | Removes humid air from around the leaf |
| More **light** | Faster | Stomata open wider for photosynthesis |

**Measuring:** a **potometer** measures water **uptake** (bubble moves along a scale); rate = distance ÷ time. Cut the shoot under water and keep joints airtight so no air enters the xylem.

**Wilting:** when water loss exceeds uptake, cells lose turgor and the leaves droop; stomata close, which reduces further loss.

**Why plants need transpiration:** it delivers water for photosynthesis and mineral ions, keeps cells turgid, and evaporation **cools** the leaf.

# 8.4 Adaptations

- **Reducing water loss:** waxy cuticle, stomata mostly on the lower surface, fewer stomata, sunken or hairy stomata (xerophytes like cacti), rolled leaves, small leaves/spines, thick stems to store water.
- **Stomata** open in the light when guard cells take in water (turgid, curved) and close in the dark or when the plant is short of water.

notes:
# Diffusion

**Definition:** the net movement of particles from a region of their **higher concentration** to a region of their **lower concentration**, down a concentration gradient, as a result of their random movement.

- Needs **no energy** from the cell (passive).
- Examples: oxygen into cells, carbon dioxide out of cells, oxygen into blood in the lungs.

**Factors that increase the rate of diffusion**

1. Larger **surface area**
2. Higher **temperature** (particles move faster)
3. Steeper **concentration gradient**
4. Shorter **distance** (thinner membrane)

# Osmosis

**Definition:** the net movement of **water molecules** from a region of higher water potential (dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (concentrated solution), through a **partially permeable membrane**.

| Solution around cell | Animal cell | Plant cell |
|---|---|---|
| Dilute (water enters) | Swells and may **burst** (lysis) | Becomes **turgid** — cell wall stops bursting |
| Same concentration | No change | No change |
| Concentrated (water leaves) | Shrinks, **crenated** | **Flaccid**, then **plasmolysed** (membrane pulls away from wall) |

> Turgor pressure keeps plants upright. Wilting = cells lose water and become flaccid.

**Osmosis experiment:** potato cylinders in different sucrose concentrations → measure mass change. Gain in mass = water entered (solution more dilute than cell); loss = water left. Where the line crosses zero change, the solution has the same concentration as the potato.

# Active transport

**Definition:** the movement of particles through a cell membrane from a region of **lower** concentration to a region of **higher** concentration (against the gradient) **using energy from respiration**.

- Uses **carrier proteins** in the membrane.
- Examples: root hair cells absorbing mineral ions from soil; glucose absorbed in the small intestine.
- Cells doing lots of active transport have **many mitochondria**.

## Comparing the three

| | Diffusion | Osmosis | Active transport |
|---|---|---|---|
| What moves | Any particles | Water only | Ions/molecules |
| Direction | High → low | High water potential → low | Low → high |
| Energy needed | No | No | Yes (ATP) |
| Membrane needed | No | Yes, partially permeable | Yes, with carrier proteins |

notes:
# Inside the atom

| Particle | Relative mass | Relative charge | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| Proton | 1 | +1 | Nucleus |
| Neutron | 1 | 0 | Nucleus |
| Electron | 1/1840 (≈ 0) | −1 | Shells around nucleus |

- **Proton (atomic) number Z** = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom.
- **Nucleon (mass) number A** = protons + neutrons.
- Neutrons = A − Z.

Notation: ²³₁₁Na → 11 protons, 11 electrons, 23 − 11 = 12 neutrons.

## Isotopes

Atoms of the **same element** (same number of protons) with **different numbers of neutrons**. E.g. ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl. Isotopes have identical chemical properties because they have the same electron arrangement.

**Relative atomic mass (Ar)** is the weighted average of the isotopes. Chlorine: 75% ³⁵Cl, 25% ³⁷Cl → Ar = (35×75 + 37×25)/100 = 35.5.

## Electron shells

Electrons fill the shells nearest the nucleus first: **2, 8, 8** (for the first 20 elements).

| Element | Z | Electronic configuration |
|---|---|---|
| Lithium | 3 | 2,1 |
| Carbon | 6 | 2,4 |
| Neon | 10 | 2,8 |
| Sodium | 11 | 2,8,1 |
| Chlorine | 17 | 2,8,7 |
| Calcium | 20 | 2,8,8,2 |

> **Outer-shell electrons = group number.** Number of shells = period number. Noble gases have full outer shells → unreactive.

## The periodic table

- Arranged in order of **increasing proton number**.
- **Groups** (columns): same number of outer electrons → similar chemical properties.
- **Periods** (rows): same number of shells.
- Metals on the left/centre, non-metals on the right; the stepped line separates them.
- Group I = alkali metals (very reactive, reactivity **increases** down the group).
- Group VII = halogens (reactivity **decreases** down the group; more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt).
- Group VIII/0 = noble gases (unreactive, full outer shell).
- Transition elements: hard, dense, high melting points, coloured compounds, act as catalysts, variable oxidation states.

notes:
# Why atoms bond

Atoms react to get a **full outer shell** (like a noble gas). They can **lose**, **gain** or **share** electrons.

# Ions and ionic bonding

An **ion** is an atom (or group of atoms) that has lost or gained electrons and so has a charge.

- **Metals lose** electrons → **positive ions (cations)**: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻
- **Non-metals gain** electrons → **negative ions (anions)**: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻; O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻

| Group | Electrons in outer shell | Ion formed |
|---|---|---|
| I | 1 | 1+ (Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺) |
| II | 2 | 2+ (Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺) |
| III | 3 | 3+ (Al³⁺) |
| V | 5 | 3− (N³⁻) |
| VI | 6 | 2− (O²⁻, S²⁻) |
| VII | 7 | 1− (F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻) |

**Ionic bond** = the strong electrostatic attraction between **oppositely charged ions**. Formed between a **metal and a non-metal**.

Example NaCl: sodium (2,8,1) gives 1 electron to chlorine (2,8,7) → Na⁺ (2,8) and Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Draw dot-and-cross diagrams showing only the outer shells, the charges in square brackets.

Example MgO: Mg (2,8,2) gives 2 electrons to O (2,6) → Mg²⁺ and O²⁻.

**Working out ionic formulae:** charges must cancel. Ca²⁺ + Cl⁻ → CaCl₂. Al³⁺ + O²⁻ → Al₂O₃ (swap the charges as subscripts).

## Properties of ionic compounds (giant ionic lattice)

- **High melting and boiling points** — many strong ionic bonds need lots of energy to break.
- **Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved** (ions free to move) but **not when solid** (ions fixed in the lattice).
- Often soluble in water; hard, brittle crystals.

# Covalent bonding

A **covalent bond** = a shared pair of electrons between two **non-metal** atoms. Each atom counts the shared pair as its own.

| Molecule | Bonds | Outer-shell picture |
|---|---|---|
| H₂ | 1 single | H:H |
| Cl₂ | 1 single | each Cl shares 1 pair, keeps 3 lone pairs |
| H₂O | 2 single | O shares one pair with each H, 2 lone pairs |
| CH₄ | 4 single | C shares a pair with each of 4 H |
| NH₃ | 3 single | N shares with 3 H, 1 lone pair |
| HCl | 1 single | |
| O₂ | 1 double (2 shared pairs) | O=O |
| CO₂ | 2 double | O=C=O |
| N₂ | 1 triple (3 shared pairs) | N≡N |

## Properties of simple molecular (covalent) substances

- **Low melting and boiling points** — the covalent bonds are strong, but the forces **between molecules** (intermolecular forces) are weak and easily overcome. Many are gases or liquids at room temperature.
- **Do not conduct electricity** — no ions or free electrons.

## Giant covalent structures

| | Diamond | Graphite |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | Each C bonded to **4** others, tetrahedral, giant 3-D lattice | Each C bonded to **3** others in flat layers of hexagons; weak forces between layers |
| Hardness | Very hard | Soft, slippery — layers slide |
| Conducts? | No (no free electrons) | Yes — each C has one delocalised electron |
| Uses | Cutting tools, drills | Lubricant, pencils, electrodes |

Both have **very high melting points** (many strong covalent bonds). Silicon(IV) oxide (SiO₂, sand) has a diamond-like structure: each Si bonded to 4 O, each O to 2 Si.

# Metallic bonding

A lattice of **positive metal ions** in a **"sea" of delocalised electrons**; the attraction between them is the metallic bond.

- **Conduct electricity** — delocalised electrons move.
- **Malleable/ductile** — layers of ions slide over each other.
- High melting points (strong attraction).

> **Quick identification:** metal + non-metal → ionic. Non-metal + non-metal → covalent. Metal only → metallic.

notes:
# 5.1 The mole

A **mole** is the amount of substance that contains **6.02 × 10²³** particles (the Avogadro constant) — the same number of atoms as in 12 g of carbon-12.

**Molar mass** = the mass of one mole = Ar or Mr in **grams**. One mole of water (Mr 18) weighs 18 g.

> **moles = mass ÷ Mr**   (n = m / M)   → mass = moles × Mr

| Question | Working |
|---|---|
| Moles in 8 g of O₂ (Mr 32)? | 8 ÷ 32 = **0.25 mol** |
| Mass of 2 mol of CO₂ (Mr 44)? | 2 × 44 = **88 g** |
| Moles in 10 g of CaCO₃ (Mr 100)? | 10 ÷ 100 = **0.1 mol** |

# 5.2 Moles of gases

At room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.) **one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³** (24 000 cm³).

> **moles = volume (dm³) ÷ 24**   → volume = moles × 24

- 0.5 mol of H₂ = 12 dm³. 6 dm³ of CO₂ = 0.25 mol.

# 5.3 Concentration of solutions

> **concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³)**   (1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so cm³ ÷ 1000 = dm³)

- 0.2 mol NaOH in 500 cm³ → 0.2 ÷ 0.5 = **0.4 mol/dm³**.
- Concentration can also be in **g/dm³**: multiply mol/dm³ by Mr.

# 5.4 Reacting masses (using equations)

The big numbers in a balanced equation are the **mole ratio**.

**Example:** What mass of MgO forms when 6 g of Mg burns? (Mg 24, O 16)

1. Equation: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO → ratio Mg : MgO = 2 : 2 = **1 : 1**
2. Moles of Mg = 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25 mol
3. Moles of MgO = 0.25 mol (1 : 1)
4. Mass of MgO = 0.25 × 40 = **10 g**

**Example with a gas:** volume of CO₂ from 5 g of CaCO₃ at r.t.p.? CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (1 : 1). Moles = 5/100 = 0.05 → volume = 0.05 × 24 = **1.2 dm³**.

**Limiting reactant:** the one that runs out first; it decides how much product forms. The other is *in excess*.

# 5.5 Empirical and molecular formulae

- **Empirical formula:** simplest whole-number ratio of atoms (CH₂O for glucose).
- **Molecular formula:** actual numbers of atoms (C₆H₁₂O₆).

**Finding an empirical formula from masses:** divide each mass by its Ar → divide all by the smallest → whole-number ratio.

A compound contains 2.4 g of Mg and 1.6 g of O: Mg 2.4/24 = 0.1; O 1.6/16 = 0.1 → 1 : 1 → **MgO**.

1.2 g C and 0.4 g H: C 0.1, H 0.4 → 1 : 4 → **CH₄**.

**Molecular from empirical:** molecular formula Mr ÷ empirical Mr = multiplier. Empirical CH₂ (14), Mr = 42 → ×3 → **C₃H₆**.

# 5.6 Percentage yield and purity

- **% yield = actual mass obtained ÷ theoretical (calculated) mass × 100.** Less than 100% because of side reactions, losses during filtering/transfer, reversible reactions.
- **% purity = mass of pure substance ÷ mass of sample × 100.**

# 5.7 Titration calculations

25.0 cm³ of NaOH is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (1 : 1).

Moles HCl = 0.1 × 0.020 = 0.002 mol → moles NaOH = 0.002 → concentration = 0.002 ÷ 0.025 = **0.08 mol/dm³**.

notes:
# Conductors and electrolytes

- **Metals and graphite** conduct because of **delocalised electrons**; they are not changed by the current.
- **Electrolytes** are ionic compounds that conduct when **molten or dissolved** because their **ions are free to move**; they are decomposed by the current. Solid ionic compounds do not conduct.
- Covalent substances (sugar, ethanol, pure water) do not conduct.

# Electrolysis

**Definition:** the decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by the passage of an electric current.

- **Electrodes** (usually inert **graphite** or platinum): **anode = positive** electrode, **cathode = negative** electrode.
- **Cations** (positive ions, usually metals or H⁺) move to the **cathode**; **anions** (negative ions) move to the **anode**. *"PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode."*
- At the cathode ions **gain** electrons (reduction); at the anode ions **lose** electrons (oxidation). **OIL RIG**: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

## Molten compounds — simple

| Electrolyte | Cathode (−) | Anode (+) |
|---|---|---|
| Molten lead(II) bromide PbBr₂ | Lead: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb | Bromine: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ |
| Molten sodium chloride | Sodium: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na | Chlorine: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ |
| Molten aluminium oxide (with cryolite) | Aluminium: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al | Oxygen: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ |

## Aqueous solutions — water's ions compete

Water provides H⁺ and OH⁻ as well.

- **Cathode:** the **less reactive** element is discharged. Metals below hydrogen in the reactivity series (Cu, Ag) are deposited; if the metal is more reactive (Na, K, Mg…), **hydrogen** is given off: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
- **Anode:** if a **halide** (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) is present in a concentrated solution, the **halogen** forms; otherwise **oxygen** forms from hydroxide: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻.

| Electrolyte (aqueous) | Cathode | Anode | Left in solution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Concentrated NaCl (brine) | Hydrogen | Chlorine | Sodium hydroxide |
| Dilute sulfuric acid | Hydrogen | Oxygen | (ratio 2 : 1 by volume) |
| Copper(II) sulfate (graphite electrodes) | Copper | Oxygen | Solution goes paler, becomes acidic |
| Copper(II) sulfate (**copper** electrodes) | Copper deposited | Copper anode **dissolves** | Solution stays blue — used for **purification of copper** |

**Tests for the gases:** hydrogen — lit splint gives a squeaky pop; oxygen — relights a glowing splint; chlorine — bleaches damp blue litmus paper.

# Uses

- **Extraction of aluminium** from bauxite (aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite to lower the melting point; carbon anodes burn away as CO₂ forms).
- **Electrolysis of brine** → hydrogen, chlorine, sodium hydroxide (all industrially useful).
- **Electroplating:** object to be plated = **cathode**; plating metal = **anode**; electrolyte contains ions of the plating metal (e.g. silver nitrate for silver plating). Purpose: appearance and corrosion protection.
- **Purification of copper** (copper electrodes, copper sulfate solution).

# Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell

Hydrogen and oxygen react to produce **electricity and water** only (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). Advantages: no CO₂, quiet, efficient. Disadvantages: hydrogen is explosive and hard to store; producing hydrogen may use fossil fuels; few filling stations.

notes:
# Exothermic and endothermic reactions

| | Exothermic | Endothermic |
|---|---|---|
| Energy | **Released** to the surroundings | **Absorbed** from the surroundings |
| Temperature of surroundings | **Rises** | **Falls** |
| ΔH (enthalpy change) | **Negative** | **Positive** |
| Examples | Combustion, neutralisation, respiration, metals + acid, hand warmers, rusting | Thermal decomposition (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂), photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate (cold packs), electrolysis |

# Energy level (reaction pathway) diagrams

- Vertical axis = energy; horizontal = progress of reaction.
- **Exothermic:** products are **lower** than reactants; ΔH is negative (arrow down).
- **Endothermic:** products are **higher** than reactants; ΔH is positive (arrow up).
- The "hump" between them is the **activation energy (Eₐ)**: the **minimum energy that colliding particles must have to react**. It is measured from the reactants up to the top of the hump.
- A **catalyst** lowers the activation energy (provides an alternative pathway) — it does **not** change ΔH.

# Bond energies — why reactions release or absorb energy

- **Breaking bonds needs energy** (endothermic).
- **Making bonds releases energy** (exothermic).
- **ΔH = energy in (bonds broken) − energy out (bonds formed)**
  - If more energy is released making new bonds than was used breaking old ones → exothermic (ΔH negative).
  - If more energy is needed to break bonds than is released → endothermic (ΔH positive).

**Worked example:** H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Bond energies (kJ/mol): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431.

- Bonds broken: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ
- Bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ
- ΔH = 678 − 862 = **−184 kJ/mol** → exothermic

**Example 2:** CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Broken: 4 C–H (4 × 413) + 2 O=O (2 × 498) = 1652 + 996 = 2648. Formed: 2 C=O (2 × 805) + 4 O–H (4 × 464) = 1610 + 1856 = 3466. ΔH = 2648 − 3466 = **−818 kJ/mol**.

# Measuring energy changes

- Measure the temperature change of a known volume of solution in an insulated cup (calorimetry).
- **Energy (J) = mass of water (g) × 4.2 × temperature rise (°C)**   (4.2 J/g°C is the specific heat capacity of water).
- Example: 50 g of solution rises by 6 °C → 50 × 4.2 × 6 = 1260 J.

# Fuels

- A **fuel** is a substance that releases energy when burned. Fossil fuels: coal, oil, natural gas (methane). **Hydrogen** as a fuel: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O — only water is produced, no CO₂, but it is explosive and hard to store.
- **Radioactive isotopes** (uranium-235) release energy by nuclear fission — not a chemical reaction.
- **Combustion** is always exothermic; complete combustion of a hydrocarbon: hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.

notes:
# Reversible reactions

Some reactions can go both ways, shown by **⇌**. The forward reaction makes products; the backward reaction re-forms reactants.

**Examples**

- **Hydrated copper(II) sulfate:** CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue) ⇌ CuSO₄ (white) + 5H₂O. Heating drives water off (endothermic, turns white); adding water re-forms the blue hydrated salt (exothermic, gets hot). Used as a **test for water** (white → blue).
- **Cobalt(II) chloride paper:** blue (anhydrous) ⇌ pink (hydrated) — also a test for water.
- **Ammonium chloride:** NH₄Cl(s) ⇌ NH₃(g) + HCl(g) on heating; recombines on cooling.
- If the forward reaction is exothermic, the backward reaction is **endothermic by the same amount**.

# Dynamic equilibrium

In a **closed system** (nothing can enter or leave) a reversible reaction reaches **equilibrium**:

- The **forward and backward reactions happen at the same rate**.
- The **concentrations of reactants and products stay constant** (not necessarily equal).
- It is **dynamic**: both reactions are still going on, they just cancel out.

# Le Chatelier's principle

> If a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium **moves to oppose the change**.

| Change | Equilibrium shifts | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Increase concentration** of a reactant | To the **right** (more product) | Uses up the extra reactant |
| Remove a product | To the right | Replaces the product |
| **Increase temperature** | In the **endothermic** direction | Absorbs the extra heat |
| Decrease temperature | In the **exothermic** direction | Releases heat |
| **Increase pressure** (gases) | To the side with **fewer gas molecules** | Reduces the pressure |
| Decrease pressure | To the side with more gas molecules | |
| Add a **catalyst** | **No shift** — equilibrium reached faster | Speeds both reactions equally |

# The Haber process — making ammonia

**N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)**   ΔH = −92 kJ/mol (forward reaction exothermic)

- **Raw materials:** nitrogen from the **air** (fractional distillation of liquid air); hydrogen from **natural gas (methane) and steam** or cracking hydrocarbons.
- **Conditions:** **450 °C**, **200 atmospheres**, **iron catalyst**.
- Why these? 
  - **Pressure:** 4 gas molecules → 2, so high pressure pushes equilibrium right and increases rate; but very high pressure is expensive and dangerous → 200 atm is a compromise.
  - **Temperature:** the forward reaction is exothermic, so a **low** temperature gives a higher yield, but the rate would be too slow; 450 °C is a **compromise** between yield and rate.
  - **Catalyst:** iron speeds up reaching equilibrium without changing the yield.
- The ammonia is **cooled and liquefied**; unreacted N₂ and H₂ are **recycled**. Yield per pass ≈ 15%.
- **Uses of ammonia:** fertilisers (ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulfate), nitric acid, explosives, cleaning products.

# The Contact process — making sulfuric acid

1. Sulfur burned in air: S + O₂ → SO₂.
2. **2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃** — **450 °C, 1–2 atm, vanadium(V) oxide (V₂O₅) catalyst**. Forward reaction exothermic; low pressure is enough because the yield is already ~98%.
3. SO₃ absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ to give oleum, then diluted with water → H₂SO₄ (adding SO₃ directly to water is too violent).

**Uses of sulfuric acid:** fertilisers (superphosphate), detergents, car batteries, paints, dyes, processing metals.

# Fertilisers (link)

Plants need **N** (leaf growth, made into proteins), **P** (roots), **K** (flowers, fruit, disease resistance) — "NPK". Ammonium salts and nitrates supply N. Overuse causes **eutrophication**: fertiliser washes into rivers → algae bloom → algae die → bacteria use up oxygen → fish die.

notes:
# 4.1 Chemical formulae

A **formula** shows which elements are in a substance and how many atoms of each. H₂O = 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen. Ca(OH)₂ = 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H (the subscript outside the bracket multiplies everything inside).

## Elements that exist as molecules

H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ — "**HOFBrINCl**". Also P₄ and S₈. All other elements are written as single atoms (Na, Fe, He).

## Common ions — learn these

| Positive (cations) | | Negative (anions) | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sodium | Na⁺ | Chloride | Cl⁻ |
| Potassium | K⁺ | Bromide | Br⁻ |
| Silver | Ag⁺ | Iodide | I⁻ |
| Ammonium | NH₄⁺ | Hydroxide | OH⁻ |
| Hydrogen | H⁺ | Nitrate | NO₃⁻ |
| Magnesium | Mg²⁺ | Hydrogencarbonate | HCO₃⁻ |
| Calcium | Ca²⁺ | Oxide | O²⁻ |
| Copper(II) | Cu²⁺ | Sulfide | S²⁻ |
| Zinc | Zn²⁺ | Sulfate | SO₄²⁻ |
| Iron(II) | Fe²⁺ | Carbonate | CO₃²⁻ |
| Iron(III) | Fe³⁺ | Phosphate | PO₄³⁻ |
| Aluminium | Al³⁺ | Nitride | N³⁻ |

Roman numerals show the charge of a transition metal ion: iron(III) = Fe³⁺.

## Writing ionic formulae — "swap and drop"

The total positive charge must equal the total negative charge.

- Sodium chloride: Na⁺ Cl⁻ → **NaCl**
- Magnesium chloride: Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ → **MgCl₂**
- Aluminium oxide: Al³⁺ O²⁻ → swap the numbers → **Al₂O₃**
- Calcium nitrate: Ca²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻ → **Ca(NO₃)₂** (brackets around a polyatomic ion when there is more than one)
- Ammonium sulfate: NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ → **(NH₄)₂SO₄**

## Covalent compounds

The name often tells you: carbon **di**oxide CO₂, carbon **mon**oxide CO, sulfur **di**oxide SO₂, dinitrogen tetroxide N₂O₄. Learn: water H₂O, ammonia NH₃, methane CH₄, hydrogen chloride HCl, ethanol C₂H₅OH, glucose C₆H₁₂O₆.

# 4.2 Chemical equations

**Word equation:** magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide

**Symbol equation:** 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

## Balancing

Atoms are never created or destroyed in a reaction (conservation of mass), so there must be the **same number of each type of atom on both sides**. You may only change the **big numbers in front** of formulas, never the small subscripts.

Method:
1. Write the correct formulas (unbalanced).
2. Count each element on both sides.
3. Add big numbers to balance, one element at a time — leave hydrogen and oxygen till last.
4. Re-count everything.

```
CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O        (H: 4 vs 2, O: 2 vs 3)
CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O       (H balanced; O: 2 vs 4)
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O      ✓

Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃
4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃          ✓ (Al 4=4, O 6=6)

Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂
2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂     ✓
```

## State symbols

**(s)** solid · **(l)** liquid · **(g)** gas · **(aq)** aqueous (dissolved in water)

2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)

## Ionic equations

Show only the ions that actually change; **spectator ions** (unchanged) are left out.

Full: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq)
Ionic: **Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)** (Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators)

Neutralisation is always: **H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)**

# 4.3 Relative formula mass (Mr)

Add up the Ar of every atom. (Ar: H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Ca 40, Fe 56, Cu 64)

- H₂O = 2(1) + 16 = **18**
- CO₂ = 12 + 2(16) = **44**
- Ca(OH)₂ = 40 + 2(16 + 1) = **74**
- (NH₄)₂SO₄ = 2(14 + 4) + 32 + 4(16) = **132**

**Percentage by mass** of an element = (total Ar of that element in the formula ÷ Mr) × 100. Oxygen in H₂O: 16/18 × 100 = **88.9%**.

notes:
# Definitions for the first units

## States of matter

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Melting** | Change from solid to liquid at the melting point |
| **Boiling** | Change from liquid to gas at the boiling point, throughout the liquid |
| **Evaporation** | Change from liquid to gas from the surface only, below the boiling point |
| **Condensation** | Change from gas to liquid |
| **Freezing** | Change from liquid to solid |
| **Sublimation** | Change directly from solid to gas (or gas to solid) |
| **Kinetic particle theory** | All matter is made of particles that are constantly moving; the higher the temperature, the faster they move |
| **Diffusion** | The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, due to random motion |

## Atoms and elements

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Atom** | The smallest particle of an element that can exist |
| **Element** | A substance made of only one type of atom; cannot be broken down by chemical means |
| **Compound** | A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio |
| **Mixture** | Two or more substances not chemically bonded, in any proportion, separable by physical means |
| **Molecule** | Two or more atoms chemically bonded together (H₂, H₂O) |
| **Proton number (atomic number)** | The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom |
| **Nucleon number (mass number)** | The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus |
| **Isotopes** | Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons |
| **Relative atomic mass (Ar)** | The average mass of the isotopes of an element compared to 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom |
| **Relative molecular mass (Mr)** | The sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule |
| **Electronic configuration** | The arrangement of electrons in shells, e.g. 2,8,1 |
| **Group** | A vertical column of the periodic table; elements have the same number of outer electrons |
| **Period** | A horizontal row; elements have the same number of electron shells |
| **Noble gases** | Group VIII elements; unreactive because they have full outer shells |

## Bonding

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ion** | An atom or group of atoms with a charge, formed by losing or gaining electrons |
| **Cation** | A positive ion (formed by metals losing electrons) |
| **Anion** | A negative ion (formed by non-metals gaining electrons) |
| **Ionic bond** | The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions |
| **Covalent bond** | A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms |
| **Metallic bond** | The attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons |
| **Delocalised electron** | An electron not attached to one particular atom, free to move through the structure |
| **Intermolecular forces** | The weak forces of attraction between molecules |
| **Giant lattice** | A regular repeating 3-D arrangement of very many particles (ions or atoms) |

## Separation and purity

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Solvent** | The liquid in which a solute dissolves |
| **Solute** | The substance that dissolves |
| **Solution** | A solute dissolved in a solvent |
| **Saturated solution** | A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature |
| **Residue** | The solid left on the filter paper |
| **Filtrate** | The liquid that passes through the filter paper |
| **Pure substance** | A single element or compound, not mixed with anything else; has a sharp melting/boiling point |
| **Rf value** | Distance moved by the substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent front |
| **Locating agent** | A chemical used to show up colourless substances on a chromatogram |
| **Miscible** | Liquids that mix completely (ethanol and water); **immiscible** = form separate layers (oil and water) |

notes:
# Elements, compounds, mixtures

- **Element:** one type of atom only (O₂, Fe, He). Cannot be broken down chemically.
- **Compound:** two or more elements **chemically bonded** in a fixed ratio (H₂O, NaCl). Properties differ from its elements; needs a chemical reaction to separate.
- **Mixture:** substances **not chemically bonded**, in any proportion (air, sea water, alloys). Can be separated by physical methods; each part keeps its own properties.

> **Pure substance** = one element or one compound only. A pure substance has a **sharp** melting/boiling point; impurities lower the m.p. and raise the b.p. and spread it over a range.

# Separation techniques

| Technique | Separates | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Filtration | Insoluble solid from liquid | Sand from water |
| Evaporation / crystallisation | Soluble solid from solution | Salt from salt water; copper sulfate crystals |
| Simple distillation | Solvent from a solution | Pure water from sea water |
| Fractional distillation | Liquids with **different boiling points** | Ethanol from water; crude oil |
| Paper chromatography | Dissolved substances (dyes, inks) | Colours in food dye |
| Separating funnel | Immiscible liquids | Oil and water |
| Magnet | Magnetic solid | Iron filings from sulfur |

**Key words:** solvent (the liquid), solute (what dissolves), solution, residue (stays on the filter paper), filtrate (passes through), saturated solution (no more solute can dissolve).

## Distillation details

- Thermometer bulb sits at the **side arm** to measure the vapour temperature.
- Condenser: cold water enters at the **bottom** and leaves at the top.
- Fractional distillation uses a **fractionating column**; the liquid with the lowest b.p. comes off first.

## Paper chromatography

1. Draw the baseline in **pencil** (ink would dissolve and run).
2. Put a spot of the mixture on the line; stand the paper in solvent **below** the line.
3. Solvent rises; more soluble substances travel further.
4. **Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent** (always < 1, no units).
5. A pure substance gives **one spot**. Colourless substances are shown with a **locating agent**.

notes:
# The three states of matter

| | Solid | Liquid | Gas |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arrangement | Regular, closely packed | Close together, random | Far apart, random |
| Movement | Vibrate about fixed positions | Slide past each other | Move fast and freely in all directions |
| Forces between particles | Strong | Weaker | Very weak / negligible |
| Shape | Fixed | Takes shape of container | Fills the container |
| Volume | Fixed | Fixed | Not fixed (compressible) |

## Changes of state

- **Melting** solid → liquid (at the *melting point*)
- **Freezing** liquid → solid
- **Boiling** liquid → gas (at the *boiling point*), throughout the liquid
- **Evaporation** liquid → gas from the surface only, at any temperature
- **Condensation** gas → liquid
- **Sublimation** solid → gas directly (e.g. dry ice, iodine)

> During a change of state the **temperature stays constant** — the energy goes into breaking (or forming) the forces between particles, not into moving them faster. This gives the flat parts on a heating/cooling curve.

## Kinetic particle theory

All matter is made of tiny particles that are constantly moving. Higher temperature → more kinetic energy → faster movement.

**Effect of temperature and pressure on gases**

- Heating a gas: particles move faster, hit the walls harder and more often → **pressure increases** (fixed volume) or **volume increases** (fixed pressure).
- Compressing a gas: particles closer together → more collisions with the walls → **pressure increases**.

## Diffusion

The net movement of particles from a region of **higher concentration** to a region of **lower concentration** because of their random motion. No energy input needed.

- Evidence: bromine vapour spreads through a gas jar; potassium manganate(VII) colour spreads through water.
- **Lighter molecules diffuse faster.** Classic experiment: ammonia (Mr 17) and hydrogen chloride (Mr 36.5) in a tube — the white ring of ammonium chloride forms **closer to the HCl end** because NH₃ travels faster.
- Diffusion is faster at higher temperatures.

notes:
# Measuring rate

**Rate = amount of reactant used (or product formed) ÷ time.**

Ways to measure:

- **Volume of gas** collected in a gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder over time (e.g. Mg + HCl → H₂).
- **Loss of mass** on a balance as a gas escapes (cotton wool in the flask neck) — e.g. marble chips + acid → CO₂.
- **Time for a cross to disappear** (sodium thiosulfate + HCl → cloudy sulfur precipitate); rate ∝ 1/time.
- Colour change, pH change, temperature change.

**Graphs of amount of product vs time:** steep at the start (most reactant, most collisions), gradient decreases, then **flat when the reaction is finished** (a reactant is used up). The **gradient = rate**. A faster reaction gives a steeper line that levels off sooner at the **same** final amount (if the same amount of limiting reactant).

# Collision theory

For a reaction to happen, particles must **collide** with **enough energy** (at least the **activation energy**) and in the right orientation. Rate increases if collisions are **more frequent** or **more energetic**.

# Factors affecting rate

| Factor | Effect | Explanation (write both parts!) |
|---|---|---|
| **Concentration** (solutions) ↑ | Rate ↑ | More particles per unit volume → **more frequent collisions** |
| **Pressure** (gases) ↑ | Rate ↑ | Particles closer together → more frequent collisions |
| **Temperature** ↑ | Rate ↑ (roughly doubles per 10 °C) | Particles move faster → collisions **more frequent** AND **more energetic**, so more collisions have ≥ activation energy |
| **Surface area** ↑ (smaller pieces, powder) | Rate ↑ | More particles exposed on the surface → more frequent collisions |
| **Catalyst** added | Rate ↑ | Provides an alternative route with **lower activation energy**, so more collisions are successful; catalyst not used up |
| Light (photochemical reactions) | Rate ↑ | e.g. photosynthesis, silver salts in photographic film |

> **Temperature is the only factor that changes the energy of collisions.** Concentration, pressure and surface area only change the frequency.

# Catalysts

- Speed up a reaction without being used up (the same mass is left at the end).
- Lower the activation energy.
- Examples: manganese(IV) oxide decomposing hydrogen peroxide; iron in the Haber process; **enzymes** (biological catalysts, e.g. in yeast fermentation); catalytic converters in cars (platinum).

# Explosions from powders

Flour, coal dust and custard powder can explode in factories and mines because the tiny particles have a huge surface area, so combustion is extremely fast.

# Typical practical: marble chips and hydrochloric acid

CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Compare large chips vs small chips vs powder with the same mass and the same acid: measure CO₂ volume every 30 s. Powder reacts fastest. **Control variables:** mass of marble, volume and concentration of acid, temperature.

notes:
# Oxidation and reduction — four ways to define them

| | Oxidation | Reduction |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | **Gain** of oxygen | **Loss** of oxygen |
| Hydrogen | Loss of hydrogen | Gain of hydrogen |
| Electrons | **Loss** of electrons | **Gain** of electrons (**OIL RIG**) |
| Oxidation state | **Increases** | **Decreases** |

Oxidation and reduction always happen **together** → a **redox** reaction.

**Examples**

- 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO: magnesium gains oxygen (oxidised); Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ loses electrons (oxidised); O gains electrons (reduced).
- CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O: copper oxide loses oxygen (reduced); hydrogen gains oxygen (oxidised).
- Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (blast furnace): iron oxide reduced, carbon monoxide oxidised.
- Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu (displacement): Zn loses electrons (oxidised), Cu²⁺ gains electrons (reduced).

# Oxidising and reducing agents

- **Oxidising agent:** oxidises something else and is itself **reduced** (gains electrons). Examples: oxygen, chlorine, **acidified potassium manganate(VII)** (purple → colourless), **potassium dichromate(VI)** (orange → green), hydrogen peroxide.
- **Reducing agent:** reduces something else and is itself **oxidised** (loses electrons). Examples: hydrogen, carbon, carbon monoxide, reactive metals, **potassium iodide** (colourless → brown as iodine forms).

**Tests:** acidified KMnO₄ turns from purple to colourless in the presence of a reducing agent; KI solution turns brown (iodine) in the presence of an oxidising agent.

# Oxidation states (oxidation numbers)

Rules:

1. Uncombined element = **0** (Fe, O₂, Cl₂).
2. Simple ion = its charge (Na⁺ = +1, Cl⁻ = −1, Al³⁺ = +3).
3. In compounds: Group I metals +1, Group II +2, **hydrogen +1** (except metal hydrides −1), **oxygen −2** (except peroxides −1), fluorine −1.
4. The oxidation states in a neutral compound **add to 0**; in a polyatomic ion they add to the **ion's charge**.

Worked: Fe₂O₃ → O is −2 × 3 = −6, so 2Fe = +6, Fe = **+3**. MnO₄⁻ → 4 O = −8; total = −1 → Mn = **+7**. SO₄²⁻ → S = +6. Roman numerals in names give the oxidation state: iron(III) chloride FeCl₃, copper(II) oxide CuO, manganese(IV) oxide MnO₂.

**Identifying redox with oxidation states:** in Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂, Zn goes 0 → +2 (oxidised), H goes +1 → 0 (reduced).

# Half-equations and ionic equations

A redox reaction can be split into two **half-equations** showing the electrons:

- Oxidation: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
- Reduction: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
- Add them (electrons cancel): Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu

At the electrodes in electrolysis: cathode = reduction (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu), anode = oxidation (2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻).

# Everyday redox

- **Combustion** (fuel oxidised), **rusting** (iron oxidised: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃; needs oxygen AND water), **respiration**, **bleaching** (oxidising agents), **metal extraction** (ores reduced with carbon or by electrolysis), **batteries** (electrons flow from the oxidised to the reduced substance).

notes:
# Why binary?

Computers use **binary** (base 2) because the hardware is made of switches/transistors that are either **on (1)** or **off (0)**. One binary digit is a **bit**; 8 bits = 1 **byte**; 4 bits = a **nibble**.

# Binary ↔ denary

Place values for 8 bits:

| 128 | 64 | 32 | 16 | 8 | 4 | 2 | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Binary → denary:** add the place values under each 1. `10110010` = 128+32+16+2 = **178**.
- **Denary → binary:** subtract the biggest place value you can, repeat. 205 → 128 (77 left) → 64 (13) → 8 (5) → 4 (1) → 1 → `11001101`.
- Biggest 8-bit number = 255 (all ones). An n-bit register holds 2ⁿ values (0 to 2ⁿ − 1).

# Binary addition

Rules: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=**10** (write 0 carry 1), 1+1+1=**11** (write 1 carry 1).

```
  0 1 1 0 1 1 0 1   (109)
+ 0 0 1 1 0 1 1 0   ( 54)
-----------------
  1 0 1 0 0 0 1 1   (163)
```

**Overflow:** if the answer needs more bits than the register has (e.g. 9 bits in an 8-bit register), the carry is lost → wrong result.

# Hexadecimal (base 16)

Digits **0–9, A–F** (A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15). Each hex digit = **one nibble (4 bits)**.

- **Binary → hex:** split into groups of 4 from the right. `1011 0110` → B 6 → **B6**.
- **Hex → binary:** each digit to 4 bits. 3F → 0011 1111.
- **Hex → denary:** place values 16, 1. 2A = 2×16 + 10 = **42**.

**Why programmers use hex:** shorter and easier to read/remember than long binary strings, fewer errors, easy to convert (1 digit = 4 bits). Used in: colour codes (#FF0000), MAC addresses, memory addresses, error messages, HTML.

# Logical shifts

- **Left shift** by 1 = multiply by 2. `00001100` (12) → `00011000` (24).
- **Right shift** by 1 = divide by 2 (integer). `00001100` → `00000110` (6).
- Bits shifted off the end are lost; zeros fill in.

# Two's complement (negative numbers)

The leftmost bit is worth **−128**. To negate: flip all bits, add 1. −5 → 5 = 00000101 → flip 11111010 → +1 = **11111011**. Range for 8 bits: −128 to +127.

notes:
# Storage units — how much is each one?

| Unit | Equals | In bytes | In bits |
|---|---|---|---|
| bit (b) | one 0 or 1 | 1/8 byte | 1 |
| nibble | 4 bits | ½ byte | 4 |
| byte (B) | 8 bits | 1 | 8 |
| kibibyte (KiB) | 1024 bytes (2¹⁰) | 1 024 | 8 192 |
| mebibyte (MiB) | 1024 KiB (2²⁰ bytes) | 1 048 576 | 8 388 608 |
| gibibyte (GiB) | 1024 MiB (2³⁰ bytes) | 1 073 741 824 | ≈ 8.59 × 10⁹ |
| tebibyte (TiB) | 1024 GiB (2⁴⁰ bytes) | ≈ 1.1 × 10¹² | ≈ 8.8 × 10¹² |
| pebibyte (PiB) | 1024 TiB (2⁵⁰ bytes) | ≈ 1.13 × 10¹⁵ | |
| exbibyte (EiB) | 1024 PiB (2⁶⁰ bytes) | ≈ 1.15 × 10¹⁸ | |

**Decimal prefixes** (used by hard-drive makers and in everyday speech): kilobyte KB = 1000 bytes, megabyte MB = 1000 KB = 10⁶ bytes, gigabyte GB = 10⁹ bytes, terabyte TB = 10¹² bytes.

> Cambridge exams use the **binary** units (KiB, MiB, GiB) and 1 KiB = 1024 bytes. To convert: bits ÷ 8 = bytes; bytes ÷ 1024 = KiB; KiB ÷ 1024 = MiB.

Example: 3 MiB in bits = 3 × 1024 × 1024 × 8 = **25 165 824 bits**. 40 000 bits = 5000 bytes = 5000 ÷ 1024 ≈ **4.88 KiB**.

# Text

Every character (letter, digit, symbol, space) is stored as a binary code from a **character set**.

| Character set | Bits per character | Characters | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| ASCII | 7 | 128 | English letters, digits, punctuation, control codes |
| Extended ASCII | 8 | 256 | Adds some accented letters and symbols |
| Unicode (UTF-8/16/32) | up to 32 | over 1 million | Every language: Georgian, Russian, Chinese, emoji |

- In ASCII, upper-case and lower-case letters have different codes: 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97 (they differ by 32).
- Codes are in order, so 'B' = 66, 'C' = 67 — you can work out a code from a nearby one.
- **Why Unicode?** ASCII cannot represent non-English characters. **Cost:** Unicode files are larger because each character uses more bits.

# Images (bitmaps)

A bitmap image is a grid of **pixels**; each pixel's colour is stored as a binary number.

- **Resolution** = width × height in pixels (e.g. 1920 × 1080). Higher resolution → more detail, bigger file.
- **Colour depth** = bits per pixel. 1 bit → 2 colours; 8 bits → 256 colours; 24 bits → 16.7 million colours ("true colour").
- **File size (bits) = width × height × colour depth.** Divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1024 for KiB.

Example: 800 × 600 pixels, 24-bit colour → 800 × 600 × 24 = 11 520 000 bits = 1 440 000 bytes ≈ 1406 KiB ≈ 1.37 MiB.

**Metadata** stored with the image: dimensions, colour depth, date, camera settings, GPS.

# Sound

Sound is an analogue wave; a computer stores it as a series of **samples** (measurements of the wave height).

- **Sample rate**: samples per second (Hz). CD quality = 44 100 Hz.
- **Sample resolution (bit depth)**: bits per sample. CD = 16 bits.
- Higher sample rate and resolution → more accurate sound, **bigger file**.
- **File size (bits) = sample rate × sample resolution × seconds** (× 2 for stereo).

Example: 30 s, 44 100 Hz, 16-bit, mono → 44 100 × 16 × 30 = 21 168 000 bits ≈ 2.52 MiB.

# Compression

| | Lossless | Lossy |
|---|---|---|
| Data lost? | No — original fully restored | Yes — permanently removed |
| How | Finds repeated patterns (RLE), stores them more efficiently | Removes detail humans barely notice: sounds outside hearing range, similar colours |
| Examples | PNG, GIF, ZIP, FLAC | JPEG, MP3, MP4, AAC |
| Use when | Text, program code, spreadsheets — every bit matters | Photos, music, video — small size matters more than perfection |

**Run-length encoding (RLE)** — lossless. Replace runs of the same value with (count, value):

```
WWWWWBBBWW  →  5W 3B 2W
```
Works well for images with big blocks of one colour; poorly for photos with few repeats.

**Lossy methods** in the exam: reduce resolution, reduce colour depth, reduce sample rate or resolution, remove frequencies humans can't hear (perceptual music shaping).

notes:
# 3.1 Computer architecture

**Von Neumann architecture:** a single processor, with **data and instructions stored together** in the same memory, using the **stored program** concept; instructions are fetched one at a time.

## Components of the CPU (central processing unit)

| Component | Job |
|---|---|
| **Control unit (CU)** | Decodes instructions, sends control signals, synchronises everything with the clock |
| **Arithmetic logic unit (ALU)** | Does arithmetic (+ − × ÷) and logic (AND, OR, comparisons) |
| **Registers** | Tiny, very fast storage inside the CPU |
| **Buses** | Wires carrying signals between components |

**Registers to know:**

- **PC** — Program Counter: address of the **next** instruction.
- **MAR** — Memory Address Register: the address currently being read from or written to.
- **MDR** — Memory Data Register: the data just read from or about to be written to memory.
- **CIR** — Current Instruction Register: the instruction being decoded/executed.
- **ACC** — Accumulator: holds results of ALU calculations.

**Buses:** **address bus** (carries addresses, CPU → memory, one-way), **data bus** (carries data, two-way), **control bus** (control signals, e.g. read/write, clock).

## Fetch–decode–execute cycle

1. **Fetch:** PC address copied to MAR; instruction at that address copied via the data bus into MDR, then to CIR; PC incremented.
2. **Decode:** CU decodes the instruction in the CIR.
3. **Execute:** the instruction is carried out (ALU calculates, data moved, jump changes the PC…).

## CPU performance

- **Clock speed** (GHz): cycles per second; higher = more instructions per second. **Overclocking** raises it but causes overheating/instability.
- **Cache:** small fast memory inside/near the CPU holding frequently used instructions and data → fewer slow trips to RAM.
- **Number of cores:** each core can run its own instructions; dual/quad core → more tasks at once (but not automatically 2× or 4× faster).
- **Bus width:** wider data bus moves more bits per cycle; wider address bus addresses more memory (16-bit → 2¹⁶ = 65 536 addresses).

## Instruction sets and embedded systems

- **Instruction set:** the list of all commands a CPU can process (opcode + operand).
- **Embedded system:** a computer built into a device to do a dedicated job (washing machine, car engine management, thermostat). Small, cheap, low power, hard to update, no general user interface.

# 3.2 Input and output devices

**Input:** keyboard, mouse, touch screen (resistive, capacitive, infrared), microphone, digital camera, scanner (2-D: flatbed; 3-D), barcode reader, QR code reader, sensors.

**Output:** monitor/LCD/LED screen, printers (inkjet, laser, 3-D), speakers, projectors (DLP, LCD), actuators (motors, lights, heaters — controlled by a computer).

**Sensors** (with **ADC** to convert analogue readings to digital): temperature, light, pressure, moisture/humidity, pH, motion/infrared, gas, magnetic field, acoustic, accelerometer, proximity, flow, level. Used in monitoring (report) and control (act) systems — e.g. a greenhouse: temperature sensor → microprocessor compares with set value → turns heater on/off.

# 3.3 Data storage

**Primary memory (directly accessed by the CPU):**

| | RAM | ROM |
|---|---|---|
| Full name | Random access memory | Read only memory |
| Volatile? | **Yes** — lost when power is off | **No** — permanent |
| Can be changed? | Read and write | Read only (normally) |
| Holds | Programs and data currently in use | Start-up instructions (BIOS/bootstrap), firmware |

**Secondary storage (not directly accessed by the CPU; non-volatile):**

| Type | Examples | How it works | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Magnetic** | Hard disk drive (HDD), magnetic tape | Magnetised spots on spinning platters read by a moving head | Large, cheap per GB, moving parts, slower, fragile |
| **Optical** | CD, DVD, Blu-ray | Laser reads pits and lands on a spiral track | Cheap, portable, low capacity, scratches |
| **Solid state** | SSD, USB flash drive, SD card | Flash memory: electrons trapped in floating-gate transistors (NAND) | No moving parts, fast, robust, quiet, low power, more expensive per GB, limited write cycles |

**Virtual memory:** when RAM is full, the OS uses part of the secondary storage as extra memory, swapping pages in and out. Lets larger programs run but is slow; too much swapping = **disk thrashing**.

**Cloud storage:** data stored on remote servers accessed via the internet. Pros: access anywhere, automatic backup, no need for own hardware. Cons: needs internet, security/privacy concerns, ongoing cost, dependence on the provider.

# 3.4 Network hardware

- **NIC (network interface card):** lets a device connect to a network; has a unique **MAC address** (48-bit, shown in hex, e.g. 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E; first half = manufacturer, second = device). MAC addresses are fixed; IP addresses can change.
- **IPv4:** 32-bit, four numbers 0–255 (192.168.1.10). **IPv6:** 128-bit, hexadecimal with colons — far more addresses.
- **Router:** sends packets to their destination across networks; assigns IP addresses; connects a LAN to the internet.
